final_answer:
No. The trial court did not err (and did not abuse its discretion) in disqualifying Smith Fullingham. Under Texas law, which governs this Dallas state-court dispute, a firm that employs a nonlawyer (legal assistant) who previously worked on the same matter for the opposing side is disqualified unless it took the minimal prophylactic measures the Texas Supreme Court requires, and here it did not.

Framework. Disqualification is a severe remedy, and the movant must show actual prejudice, but for side-switching nonlawyers Texas applies a two-step presumption scheme (In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010); Phoenix Founders v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994); National Medical Enterprises v. Godbey, 924 S.W.2d 123 (Tex. 1996)). Step one: there is an irrebuttable presumption that the nonlawyer obtained confidences at the prior firm. Jones's facts easily meet it: she prepared litigation documents, took part in hundreds of privileged communications and attended strategy meetings on this very case. Step two: there is a rebuttable presumption that the nonlawyer shares those confidences with the new firm. Columbia Valley holds that disqualification is always required when (a) confidences were in fact disclosed, (b) screening would be ineffective, or (c) the nonlawyer necessarily must work on the other side of the same or a substantially related matter. Otherwise, the firm avoids disqualification only if it shows formal screening that achieves the practical effect of preventing disclosure, with the nonlawyer being instructed not to work on or discuss the matter, and the firm taking timely, substantiated, institutionalized measures. Columbia Valley also treats the presumption of shared confidences as irrebuttable where the nonlawyer actually performed work, including clerical work, on the matter at the firm's direction and the lawyer reasonably should have known of the conflict. Jones did exactly that: thirteen occasions of secretarial work on Apex v. Prestige and, in March 2022, e-filing two documents under her name.

The controlling recent decision is In re Zaidi (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026, No. 24-0245), whose facts closely track this problem (a legal assistant who earlier worked for the opposing side, later worked at a firm that, years after her hire, came to represent the other side, and was assigned a few tasks, with the movant learning of it from two e-filing notifications). As I understand it from secondary summaries (I could not retrieve the full opinion), the Court held (1) the firm must instruct/admonish the nonlawyer not to work on any matter on which she worked in prior employment, at or before the time she begins work on the conflicted matter, even if the conflict arises years after hiring and even if she was not hired as a side-switcher, and that absent that minimal measure the firm is disqualified; and (2) e-filing notifications bearing her name did not conclusively establish waiver, so mandamus was denied and the disqualification order stood.

Application. (1) Smith Fullingham did not inquire about Jones's prior work on hiring in 2017 and gave her no admonition not to work on Apex-Prestige before she began working on it. The firm had a duty to screen and instruct when the conflict arose; the firm's own ignorance does not excuse it. (2) The first measures were a screen announced in January 2023, after thirteen instances of work over five years and after the March 2022 filings; that is neither timely nor formal/institutionalized, and a screen cannot cure past participation. (3) The firm's response that Jones 'did not recall' the prior work and had not shared confidences is not a rebuttal: the presumption of shared confidences is irrebuttable where she actually worked on the matter at the firm's direction, and the fact that she was assigned only limited secretarial work does not matter because Columbia Valley expressly includes clerical work. Her lack of recollection is not a substitute for the required prophylactic measures. (4) Waiver: Apex learned of the conflict in January 2023, inquired, and moved to disqualify in early March 2023, roughly two months later; under Texas law a party can waive disqualification by unreasonable delay, but the delay is measured from when the movant knew or should have known of the conflict, and Zaidi held that e-filing notifications do not conclusively establish waiver. Apex therefore has not waived, although a firm might argue constructive knowledge from the 2022 filing notifications; a fact question on this is resolved by the trial court, and the court's implicit finding of no waiver is within its discretion. (5) Standard of review: the disqualification order is reviewed for abuse of discretion, and a trial court has no discretion to refuse disqualification where the law requires it; conversely, when the law requires disqualification, granting it cannot be an abuse.

Caveats: Zaidi's text was not retrieved directly, only through search summaries; the details (especially whether the opinion reaches the irrebuttable-presumption point on these facts) should be confirmed. Also, whether disqualification of the firm is mandatory or only the 'ordinary' result does not change the outcome here because the minimum measures were never taken and Jones in fact worked on the matter. Practically, the case is on remand for a new trial, so Apex would suffer prejudice from confidences used against it; this supports the trial court's exercise of discretion.

claims.text: The trial court did not err in disqualifying Smith Fullingham; the firm took no timely admonishment/screening and Jones actually worked on the matter.

Irrebuttable presumption of shared confidences applies where the nonlawyer performed even clerical work on the same matter at the firm's direction, so her lack of recollection and limited duties do not rebut it.
Apex's roughly two-month delay after learning of the conflict, and the e-filing notifications, do not establish waiver as a matter of law.
Underlying presumption framework derives from Phoenix Founders.
